newsitem.title: USA: CBOT March corn sets fresh 4-1/2 month high, funds.
newsitem.headline: CBOT March corn sets fresh 4-1/2 month high, funds.

text.p: CBOT corn futures rallied late on aggressive fund buying with late short covering of calls in the $2.90 March strike in corn options buoying nearby March to a fresh 4-1/2 month high, traders said.
"It was a lot of options buying late," a trader said. "The options pit was short $2.90 calls and as corn rallied toward $2.90, they covered."
In late and fast trading, March reached a session high of $2.92-1/2 per bushel, the highest level since $2.95-1/4 was touched on October 16.
Fund buying totaled roughly 40 to 50 million bushels.
"These guys are relentless," said Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co, referring to fund buying. "Every day they're buying."

Funds this week purchased about 300 million bushels of corn, traders said and Friday's strong performance indicated the closely-watched managed accounts may be in for the long haul. "They're banking on a summer weather market," a trader said. Only scattered profit taking was noted Friday.
Bullish fervor also was generated by a steady stream of supportive signals from the export sector, traders said.
Corn closed 4-3/4 cents per bushel higher to 3/4 lower, with March up 4-3/4 at $2.91-3/4 a bushel.
Slow farmer selling also kept the market tone resilient.

Corn was buffeted in early dealings and fast market signs were posted in all contracts only because the neighboring soy complex edged higher on the open but quickly fell amid nervousness about talk China cancelled South American and Indian soymeal. The soy complex rattled the corn pit.
"It's about like a 40 yard grenade toss down here right now with some looking at tossing 25 yards," a trader said.
USDA early Friday said U.S. net export sales of corn during the week ended February 13 tallied 814,800 tonnes, near the top of trade expectations for 700,000 to 850,000 tonnes.

Traders also said the market remained mindful of persistent talk about dry weather in key South African maize producing areas and traders still were talking about a USDA Cattle on Feed Report released a week ago.

USDA last Friday said the seven key U.S. cattle feeding states reported cattle placements on feed during January at roughly 25 percent above a year ago. Analysts had expected closer to a seven to eight percent increase in placements.
That scenario indicated more animals consuming feed in the next few months than previously expected, and helped underpin the case for the bulls in the corn and soymeal pits.
Traders also said Japan remains unpriced on much of the corn it has booked and there was evidence of Japanese pricing on the open Friday morning.
"That higher open saw a lot of Japanese pricing," a trader said.

On the day, Merrill Lynch Futures bought five million bushels each of March and July, E.D. and F. Man International bought four million March and two million bushels each of May and July, traders said.
Cargill Inc sold two million each of May and July and Farmers Commodities Corp sold two million July and sold one million May, traders said.
Corn futures volume was estimated by the CBOT at 85,000 contracts, below the 114,968 traded Thursday.

In corn options, Refco Inc bought 1,000 May $2.70 puts at 2-3/4 cents, Smith Barney bought 1,500 December $2.40 puts at 4-3/4 cents and ADM Investor Services bought 500 May $2.70 puts at 2-3/4 cents, traders said.
Corn options volume was estimated at 30,000 contracts, about the same as the 30,335 traded Thursday.

Technicians said the longer term four- and 20-day moving averages early Friday were bullish for the corn market. But the short term nine day relative strength index (RSI) for the March gave off overdone tones at 86 percent. The market views an RSI of 70 or more as an overbought scenario and 30 or less as an oversold market.
First support for the March was $2.84 and second support was $2.78-1/2. The session low for March was $2.86.
First resistance was $2.89 and second resistance was $2.94-1/4. The session high was $2.92-1/2, a 4-1/2 month high.
